text: Course 9 covered why CSDM exists — a standard, layered model for describing services, applications, and infrastructure consistently, with a real split between Business Services and Technical Services. This lesson is about what happens to that model once it's live across an entire enterprise, for years, not what it looks like at launch.

Standing up a correct CSDM model for one engaged team is genuinely achievable, and course 9 showed you how. The real test is different: does that same model stay correct across 40 different teams, none of whom were in the original room, independently creating and updating CIs, relationships, and service mappings for years after the implementation team has moved on.

CMDB data quality doesn't hold steady by default — it erodes unless something actively pushes back. One team classifies a new application differently from another doing the same thing. A decommissioned server's relationship to a Business Service never gets removed, because removing it wasn't anyone's assigned job. Discovery and manual creation produce duplicate CIs that drift apart. A team under time pressure takes a shortcut, and that shortcut becomes the pattern everyone else copies. None of this happens all at once — the damage is cumulative.

This is the real shift at enterprise scale: an architect's CSDM responsibility isn't designing the model once and handing it off. It's designing the ongoing governance process — named stewards for each service domain, change discipline requiring review before new CI classes or relationship types get created, recurring data-quality audits rather than a one-time cleanup, and a feedback loop so a team's workaround can signal a real gap in the model instead of quietly spreading uncorrected.

CSDM data quality degrades naturally without deliberate, ongoing governance across every team that touches the CMDB. Next up: a worked data-architecture lab, pulling table design, archiving, and CSDM governance together into one real enterprise scenario.
